title: KFamily
content: **KFamily.** A k-uniform family: a collection of sets each of cardinality exactly k. This is the basic object of study — families of k-element subsets of a ground set.
mathContext: Uniform set families (or k-uniform hypergraphs) are central objects in extremal set theory. The uniformity constraint $|A_i| = k$ for all sets in the family ensures a clean combinatorial structure where the covering problem has well-defined asymptotics in k. Without uniformity, covering problems become trivially easy (use singletons) or ill-defined.

title: PairIntersects
content: **PairIntersects.** A pair {x, y} intersects a set A if x ∈ A or y ∈ A (i.e., the pair shares at least one element with A). This is the basic intersection primitive for the r-wise pair property.
mathContext: The pair intersection condition is a weak form of intersection: it requires only that one of two specific elements belongs to each set. This is weaker than requiring a common element (which would be the sunflower property) but stronger than arbitrary pairwise intersection. The pair structure adds a 2-dimensional combinatorial flavor that distinguishes this from classical covering problems.

title: HasRWisePairProperty
content: **HasRWisePairProperty.** A family has the r-wise pair property if every r sets in the family share a common pair {x, y} that intersects all r of them. This strengthens pairwise intersection to r-wise coherence.
mathContext: The r-wise pair property is a Helly-type condition: it requires that any r sets in the family are 'linked' by a common pair. As r increases, the condition becomes stronger (more sets must share a pair), which forces the family to have more structure and allows smaller covering sets. The function $f(k,r)$ quantifies exactly how much this additional structure helps. The Helly property (every $r$ sets from a family with pairwise intersections have a common point) is the classical archetype of such conditions.

title: IsCoveringSet
content: **IsCoveringSet.** A set S is a covering set for a family if S intersects every set in the family: for every Aᵢ in the family, S ∩ Aᵢ ≠ ∅. The minimum such |S| is the covering number.
mathContext:
The covering number (also called the **piercing number** or **transversal number** $	au$) is a fundamental parameter in hypergraph theory. By LP duality, $	au$ relates to the matching number $
u$ via $
u \leq 	au \leq f(
u)$ for various functions $f$ depending on the structure. For k-uniform families with the r-wise pair property, the covering number is exactly $f(k,r)$.

title: f(k,r)
content: **f(k,r).** The minimum size of a covering set guaranteed to exist for any k-uniform family with the r-wise pair property. This is the central function of Problem #644.
mathContext: The function $f(k,r)$ captures the trade-off between uniformity $k$, coherence $r$, and covering efficiency. The EFKT92 results show $f(k,r) = c_r \cdot k + O(1)$ for small $r$, with $c_3 = 2$, $c_4 = 3/2$, $c_5 = 5/4$, $c_6 = 1$. The coefficient sequence $c_r$ is decreasing, suggesting that stronger coherence conditions enable proportionally smaller covers. The problem asks whether this linear behavior persists for all $r$.

title: Known Values (EFKT92)
content: **Known exact values.** Erdős-Fon-Der-Flaass-Kostochka-Tuza (1992) determined: f(k,3) = 2k, f(k,4) = ⌊3k/2⌋, f(k,5) = ⌊5k/4⌋, f(k,6) = k. Each requires both an upper bound (covering algorithm) and matching lower bound (extremal construction).
mathContext: The exact values reveal a striking pattern of decreasing coefficients: $2, 3/2, 5/4, 1$. These can be written as $(r-1)/(r-2)$ for $r = 3, 4$ but this formula breaks at $r = 5$ (where $5/3 \neq 5/4$). The jumps suggest the coefficient depends on the structure of extremal families, which becomes more constrained as $r$ increases. For $r = 6$, reaching $f(k,6) = k$ means the covering set need not be larger than the sets themselves — a natural barrier.

title: Coefficient Sequence
content: **coefficientSequence.** The sequence c₃ = 2, c₄ = 3/2, c₅ = 5/4, c₆ = 1, representing the leading coefficient of f(k,r) ≈ cᵣ · k. The pattern suggests c₇ = 3/4.
mathContext: The coefficient sequence $c_r$ encodes the asymptotic efficiency of covering under r-wise coherence. If $c_r \to 0$ as $r \to \infty$, it would mean that sufficiently strong coherence allows sublinear covering — a remarkable property. The known values $2, 3/2, 5/4, 1$ decrease by $1/2, 1/4, 1/4$ respectively, suggesting the decrements themselves may follow a pattern. The conjecture $c_7 = 3/4$ would continue the decrease by $1/4$.

title: Question 1: f(k,7) = (3/4+o(1))k?
content: **Question 1.** Is f(k,7) = (3/4 + o(1))k? This asks whether the decreasing coefficient pattern continues to c₇ = 3/4, dropping below the natural barrier c₆ = 1.
mathContext: The transition from $c_6 = 1$ to a conjectured $c_7 = 3/4$ would cross the important threshold where the covering set becomes smaller than each individual set in the family. This sublinear regime ($c_r < 1$) means that the r-wise pair property forces enough redundancy that a proper subset of any $A_i$ suffices to cover the entire family. Proving this likely requires new extremal constructions and covering algorithms beyond those in EFKT92.

title: Question 2: General Asymptotics
content: **Question 2.** For all r ≥ 3, does f(k,r) = (cᵣ + o(1))k for some constant cᵣ? This asks whether the linear-in-k behavior persists for all r, not just the computed cases r = 3,...,6.
mathContext: If f(k,r) grows linearly in k for all r with coefficient $c_r$, the problem reduces to understanding the sequence $(c_r)_{r \geq 3}$. Sublinear growth (f(k,r) = o(k)) for large r would be even more remarkable and would connect to the sunflower lemma, which guarantees structure in large families. The question of whether $c_r \to 0$ or stabilizes at some positive constant is a deep open problem in extremal set theory.

title: Extremal Families
content: **Extremal Families.** Constructions achieving the lower bounds for f(k,r). These show the known values are tight by exhibiting k-uniform families with the r-wise pair property that cannot be covered by fewer than f(k,r) elements.
mathContext: Extremal constructions are essential for establishing exact values of $f(k,r)$. For each $r = 3, 4, 5, 6$, EFKT92 provided explicit families requiring $2k$, $\lfloor 3k/2 \rfloor$, $\lfloor 5k/4 \rfloor$, and $k$ elements respectively. These constructions typically involve partitioning the ground set and distributing elements across the partition to create families with maximal covering resistance while maintaining the r-wise pair property.

title: Monotonicity Properties
content: **Monotonicity.** f(k,r) is non-increasing in r (stronger coherence allows smaller covers) and non-decreasing in k (larger sets need larger covers). These are natural structural properties.
mathContext: The monotonicity in $r$ follows because a family with the $(r+1)$-wise pair property automatically has the $r$-wise pair property (take any $r$ sets from a set of $r+1$ and use the guaranteed pair). Thus the constraint is stronger for larger $r$, so the worst-case covering number is smaller. The monotonicity in $k$ is similarly natural: enlarging each set gives more elements to cover.

title: Sunflower Connection
content: **Sunflower Connection.** The r-wise pair property relates to the sunflower lemma (Erdős-Ko 1960). A sunflower is a family where all pairwise intersections are the same 'core.' The Erdős-Ko sunflower lemma bounds family sizes, and the pair property provides a weaker structural guarantee that still enables efficient covering.
mathContext: The **sunflower lemma** (Erdős and Rado, 1960) states that any family of more than $(r-1)^k \cdot k!$ k-element sets contains an $r$-petal sunflower. The pair property is weaker than the sunflower condition (a common pair vs. a common core), but both force structural constraints on large families. Recent breakthroughs on the sunflower conjecture (Alweiss-Lovett-Wu-Zhang 2020, improved to $(\log k)^k$) suggest that pair-intersection structures may also admit improved bounds.

title: Main Conjecture
content: **Main Conjecture.** The conjunction of Question 1 (f(k,7) = (3/4+o(1))k) and Question 2 (existence of limiting coefficients cᵣ for all r). These two questions together would establish the complete asymptotic picture of the covering function.
mathContext: Resolving both questions would determine the asymptotic structure of $f(k,r)$ as a function of two parameters. If $c_r$ exists for all $r$ and $c_r \to 0$, it would mean that arbitrarily strong r-wise coherence makes the covering problem asymptotically trivial (sublinear in $k$). If $c_r \to c_\infty > 0$, there is a fundamental barrier to efficient covering that even infinite-wise coherence cannot overcome.
